key_results: Lecture 2, p. 4: group delay is τ(ω)=-d arg H(e^{jω})/dω and can be computed without numerical phase differentiation as Re{FT{nh[n]}/FT{h[n]}}.

Lecture 2, pp. 5–6: a real FIR impulse response symmetric about α, h[n]=h[2α-n], has H(e^{jω})=A(ω)e^{-jωα} with real A and constant group delay α; antisymmetry adds a constant π/2 phase and gives generalized linear phase.
Lecture 3, p. 1: a rational all-pass response has conjugate-reciprocal pole-zero pairs and form H_AP(z)=A∏(z^{-1}-a_k*)/(1-a_kz^{-1}), |a_k|<1.
Lecture 3, p. 2: a minimum-phase system is stable and causal with a stable causal inverse; for a rational transfer function all poles and zeros lie strictly inside the unit circle.

Lecture 3, pp. 2–3: for a real rational minimum-phase system, |H(e^{jω})|²=H(z)H(1/z) on the unit circle; factoring reciprocal pairs and selecting inside-unit-circle roots recovers H uniquely up to sign/scale.

Lecture 3, pp. 4–5: any stable system can be factored as minimum-phase times all-pass (or as minimum-phase times maximum-phase and a delay); a stable causal inverse of the minimum-phase factor equalizes magnitude while leaving the all-pass phase.

Lecture 3, p. 6: every nonconstant causal all-pass factor has nonnegative group delay, so among causal systems with a fixed magnitude response the minimum-phase realization has pointwise minimum group delay.
Lecture 3, p. 6: minimum phase also minimizes energy delay: cumulative energy Σ_{m=0}^n|h_min[m]|² is at least that of every causal sequence sharing its magnitude response.
Lecture 4, pp. 1–2: ideal C/D conversion gives x[n]=x_c(nT) and X(e^{jω})=(1/T)Σ_k X_c(j(ω/T-2πk/T)); alias-free sampling requires the CT spectrum fit inside |Ω|<π/T.
Lecture 4, p. 2: ideal D/C reconstruction is x_r(t)=Σ_nx[n]sinc((t-nT)/T), equivalently ideal lowpass filtering with gain T over |Ω|≤π/T.
Lecture 4, pp. 2–3: for a bandlimited C/D–H–D/C cascade, H_eff(jΩ)=H(e^{jΩT}) on |Ω|≤π/T.
Lecture 4, p. 3: noninteger delay Δ is not a literal sequence shift; H(e^{jω})=e^{-jωΔ} has impulse response h[n]=sinc(n-Δ) and performs bandlimited interpolation, CT delay ΔT, then resampling.
Lecture 5, pp. 1–2: decimation by M obeys X_d(e^{jω})=(1/M)Σ_{i=0}^{M-1}X(e^{j(ω-2πi)/M}); alias-free decimation requires prior bandlimiting to |ω|<π/M.
Lecture 5, p. 3: expansion by L inserts L-1 zeros and produces X_e(e^{jω})=X(e^{jωL}); an interpolation lowpass removes spectral images and supplies missing values.
Lecture 5, p. 3: rational rate change L/M should interpolate before decimating so the decimator does not irreversibly alias spectral replicas.

Lecture 6, pp. 1–2: for B+1-bit uniform quantization over ±X_M, Δ=X_M2^{-B}; the additive model assumes uniform white error uncorrelated with the input, with mean zero, variance Δ²/12, and flat PSD Δ²/12.

Lecture 6, pp. 3–4: oversampling followed by ideal lowpass filtering to π/M reduces total white quantization-noise power from Δ²/12 to Δ²/(12M); doubling M is equivalent to adding one-half bit of quantizer precision.
Lecture 6, pp. 4–5: first-order error feedback gives noise transfer 1-e^{-jω}, magnitude squared 4sin²(ω/2), moving quantization noise toward high frequencies for later lowpass removal.

Lecture 7, pp. 1–2: Direct Form I separately realizes numerator and denominator; commuting the sections and merging delays yields memory-minimal Direct Form II, while transposition reverses all branches and swaps input/output without changing the transfer function.

Lecture 7, pp. 2–3: factoring into first/second-order sections yields cascade realizations; partial fractions yield parallel realizations. They are identical at infinite precision but differ under finite-word-length arithmetic.
Lecture 7, p. 3: an FIR tap-delay line with symmetric or antisymmetric coefficients can pair mirrored samples before multiplication, roughly halving multiplier count.
Lecture 7, pp. 4–5: FIR lattice stages satisfy A_{p+1}=A_p-k_{p+1}B_p and B_{p+1}=z^{-1}(B_p-k_{p+1}A_p); reversing sections produces an all-pole lattice, stable iff every |k_i|<1.

Lecture 7, pp. 6–20: coefficient quantization moves poles and zeros; high-order direct forms can push poles outside the unit circle, whereas cascaded low-order sections localize the perturbations and are substantially more robust.

Lecture 8, pp. 1–2: practical filter design approximates an ideal magnitude within passband/stopband tolerances and treats transition bands as don't-care regions; ideal brick-wall responses are noncausal and infinitely long.
Lecture 8, p. 2: the bilinear transform s=(1-z^{-1})/(1+z^{-1}) maps the analog imaginary axis to one trip around the digital unit circle, with Ω/Ω_c=tan(ω/2)/tan(ω_c/2) prewarping.
Lecture 8, pp. 3–5: digital Butterworth magnitude squared is 1/[1+(tan(ω/2)/tan(ω_c/2))^{2N}]; it is monotone/maximally flat, with all zeros at z=-1.
Lecture 8, pp. 5–7: Chebyshev Type I is equiripple in the passband and monotone in the stopband; Type II reverses those roles, and both give the same order for the same specifications.
Lecture 8, pp. 7–8: elliptic filters are equiripple in both passband and stopband and provide the lowest-order rational magnitude approximation meeting a fixed tolerance set.

PS1 solution, Problem 1.10, pp. 8–9: for narrowband pulses, each envelope is approximately scaled by |H| and delayed by τ_g at its carrier; the worked carriers 0.12π, 0.3π, and 0.5π yield gains ≈1.8, ≈1.7, 0 and delays ≈40, ≈80 samples.
PS1 solution, Problem 1.12, pp. 9–10: an FIR h[n]=1 for n=0,1,2 driven by unit white noise gives R_yy[m]={1,2,3,2,1} on m=-2…2 and P_yy=3+4cosω+2cos2ω.

PS2 solution, Problem 2.2, pp. 1–2: causality does not force nonnegative group delay, and constant positive integer group delay does not imply a pure delay; a delayed zero-phase FIR is a counterexample.

PS2 solution, Problem 2.3, pp. 2–8: reciprocal pole-zero completion makes both minimum-phase/all-pass and minimum-phase/generalized-linear-phase factorizations unique up to scale for the assigned rational H(z).

PS2 solution, Problem 2.9, pp. 11–13: exact reconstruction requires no initial aliasing, matched periods T_1=T, and an interpolation response flat on the occupied band; consistent resampling alone is equivalent to h_1(nT-n_0T_1)=δ[n-n_0] for all integers.

PS3 solution, Problem 3.2, pp. 1–2: upsampling a WSS sequence by two produces a non-WSS cyclostationary sequence; after filtering and downsampling, WSS is recovered provided the relevant polyphase energy sum converges.

PS3 solution, Problem 3.5, pp. 3–5: second-order noise shaping gives Y=z^{-1}X+(1-z^{-1})²E, output-noise PSD 16σ_e²sin⁴(ω/2), total unfiltered power 6σ_e², and lowpass in-band variance ≈σ_e²π⁴/(5M⁵).

PS4 solution, Problem 4.4, pp. 4–6: a one-multiplier all-pass section that uses the same quantized coefficient for its pole and reciprocal zero preserves the all-pass relation under quantization; independently quantizing coefficients generally does not.

PS4 solution, Problem 4.5, pp. 6–8: roundoff-noise sources must be inserted after every multiplier; transposed/equivalent structures can have equal or different output-noise power depending on which pole network each source sees.

PS4 solution, Problems 4.6–4.7, pp. 8–10: lattice stability is exposed directly by reflection coefficients—one example with |k_i|<1 is stable, while k_1=-12/5 and k_4=-2 prove the assigned fourth-order all-pole system unstable.
PS4 solution, Problem 4.8, pp. 10–12: h[n]∗h[-n] has zero-phase response |H(e^{jω})|²; h[n]+h[-n] gives 2ReH and therefore generally fails to preserve a desired magnitude.

Background Exam solution, Problems 5 and 13, pp. 2 and 4: reflecting an outside-unit-circle zero constructs the minimum-phase spectral factor and its whitening inverse; an ideal one-third-sample delay has h[n]=sinc(n-1/3).

For a desired impulse response hd[n], minimizing integral squared frequency error over causal FIR sequences supported on 0≤n≤M gives h[n]=hd[n] on that interval and zero elsewhere; by Parseval this is exactly rectangular truncation. [Lecture 9 p. 1; PS5 solution p. 1]

Windowing multiplies hd[n] in time and convolves Hd(e^jω) with W(e^jω) in frequency. Main-lobe width controls transition width, while sidelobe area controls passband/stopband ripple; increasing a rectangular window’s length narrows lobes but does not reduce ripple amplitude. [Lecture 9 pp. 1–2]

Smooth tapering trades a wider main lobe for lower sidelobes. Rectangular, Bartlett, Hann, Hamming, and Blackman windows are fixed choices; the Kaiser family exposes the tradeoff continuously through length M+1 and shape β. [Lecture 9 p. 2]

For Kaiser design with stopband attenuation A=-20log10δ, β is piecewise in A and the order estimate is M≥(A−8)/(2.285Δω); this turns ripple and transition specifications into a practical first design. [Lecture 9 p. 3]
A type-I generalized-linear-phase FIR filter has symmetric h[n], even M, and H(e^jω)=Ae(e^jω)e^(−jωM/2), where Ae is a degree-L=M/2 polynomial P(cosω). [Lecture 9 p. 4]

The alternation theorem certifies the unique minimax polynomial approximation: a degree-L optimum has at least L+2 alternating extrema of weighted error. The Parks–McClellan algorithm repeatedly solves at guessed extremals, evaluates on a dense grid, exchanges the extremals, and stops when they no longer move. [Lecture 9 pp. 4–6]

For a type-I optimum lowpass, alternations occur at both band edges, passband and stopband ripples are equal under equal weighting, and the transition is monotonic. A PS5 proof shows that any transition-band extremum consumes too many of the polynomial’s available extrema to satisfy alternation. [Lecture 9 p. 5; PS5 solution pp. 4–5]
For expansion by L, xe[n]=x[n/L] when n/L is integral and 0 otherwise, with Xe(e^jω)=X(e^jωL). For compression by M, xd[n]=x[nM] and Xd(e^jω)=(1/M)Σ(k=0 to M−1)X(e^j(ω−2πk)/M). [Lecture 10 p. 2]

The downsampling noble identity moves a filter H(z^M) across a compressor by M; the reverse direction is valid only when the high-rate filter can be written using integer powers of z^M. [Lecture 10 pp. 2–3]

Polyphase decomposition partitions h[n] into ek[n]=h[nM+k]. In a decimator, each branch can cross its compressor by the noble identity, putting every multiplication on the low-rate side without changing the input-output relation. [Lecture 10 pp. 3–5]

For an N-tap FIR preceding downsampling by M, direct filtering costs N multiplications per input-time second, whereas a polyphase low-rate implementation costs N/M under the lecture’s assumptions. [Lecture 10 pp. 4–5]
The upsampling noble identity supports the dual interpolation construction: decompose h[n] into L polyphase components and move all filters to the low-rate side of the expanders. [Lecture 11 pp. 2–3]

Efficiency is not a single scalar: moving multipliers to a low-rate side can reduce multiplies per second while adding expander blocks or delay storage. The notes explicitly require the designer to state what ‘efficient’ means. [Lecture 11 p. 2]

Parametric modeling follows three steps: choose a model and parameters, define a modeling error, and minimize it. The shard uses S-hat(z)=A/(1−Σ(k=1 to p)akz^−k), then defines error after the inverse model so optimization becomes linear. [Lecture 12 pp. 1–2]

For causal deterministic data, least-squares prediction gives the Yule–Walker equations Σ(k=1 to p)ak φs[i−k]=φs[i], i=1,…,p, or Tp ap=rp, with a symmetric Toeplitz autocorrelation matrix. [Lecture 12 pp. 3–4]

The same normal equations arise statistically when an all-pole model is driven by white noise and the inverse filter is chosen to whiten the observed process, replacing deterministic correlation by expectation. [Lecture 12 p. 4]

Levinson–Durbin obtains an order-(p+1) solution from the order-p solution by exploiting Toeplitz symmetry. With reversed correlation vector qp and coefficient vector ρp, kp+1=[φs[p+1]−qp^T ap]/[φs[0]−rp^T ap], the correction is −kp+1ρp, and the new final coefficient is kp+1. [Lecture 13 pp. 2–5]
The recursion starts at a1^(1)=φs[1]/φs[0], avoids a fresh matrix inversion at each order, and yields every lower-order model on the way to order p. [Lecture 13 pp. 2, 5]

The Levinson reflection coefficients directly parameterize all-pole/all-zero lattice realizations. If every |kα|<1, the all-pole lattice is stable—a convenient finite-precision test compared with explicitly finding direct-form poles. [Lecture 13 pp. 5–6]

Sampling a DTFT at N equally spaced frequencies produces X[k]=Σn x[n]W_N^(nk). Perfect recovery from those samples requires the signal’s occupied duration to fit within N samples; otherwise periodic replication causes time aliasing. [Lecture 15 pp. 1–3]

A period-N sequence needs only N distinct complex exponentials. Its DFS pair is X-tilde[k]=Σ(n=0 to N−1)x-tilde[n]W_N^(nk) and x-tilde[n]=(1/N)Σ(k=0 to N−1)X-tilde[k]W_N^(−nk), with both sequences periodic modulo N. [Lecture 15 pp. 3–4]

The N-point DFT of finite x[n] is the DFS of its period-N extension and equivalently samples its DTFT at ω=2πk/N. Choosing a different N, including zero padding, generally produces different DFT samples without changing the underlying DTFT. [Lecture 15 pp. 4–6]
A circular time shift x[((n−m))N] multiplies X[k] by exp(−j2πkm/N); multiplication of two DFTs corresponds to N-point circular convolution. [Lecture 15 p. 5]

N-point circular convolution equals linear convolution followed by periodic time aliasing into N samples. For sequences of lengths L and P, N≥L+P−1 makes circular and linear convolution agree. [Lecture 16 pp. 2–4]

Overlap-add filters nonoverlapping L-sample blocks using transforms of length at least L+P−1 and adds the P−1-sample overlaps. Overlap-save uses overlapping blocks, discards each block’s first P−1 aliased outputs, and retains the uncorrupted remainder. [Lecture 16 pp. 4–5]

Backward-Euler substitution s=(1−z^−1)/T maps the stable continuous-time left half-plane inside the unit circle, whereas forward Euler z=1+sT maps it left of Re(z)=1 and can turn a stable analog pole into an unstable digital pole. Both are accurate near ΩT≈0. [PS5 solution pp. 2–3]

A three-tap type-I minimax lowpass with passband edge π/3 and stopband edge π/2 is h[n]=(1/3)(δ[n]+δ[n−1]+δ[n−2]), obtained by forcing three alternating errors at π/3, π/2, and π. [PS5 solution pp. 4–5]

For a suitable even-order linear-phase equiripple FIR, adding the stopband ripple δ2 makes the zero-phase response nonnegative; spectral factorization assigns reciprocal zero pairs to a minimum-phase half-order factor, reducing length from M+1 to M/2+1 with transformed ripple bounds. [PS5 solution pp. 5–6]

A two-stage decimator can use a much wider first-stage transition band because later rate change and spectral periodicity relax its stopband edge. In the PS5 example, symmetry and low-rate computation cut steady-state work from 2535 to 284 multiplications per final output sample. [PS5 solution pp. 6–10]

In a two-channel analysis/synthesis bank with H1(e^jω)=H0(e^j(ω+π)), perfect delayed reconstruction for arbitrary stable input requires H0²(e^jω)+H1²(e^jω)=Kexp(−jndω) and H0(e^jω)H1(e^jω)=0. [PS6 solution pp. 1–3]

Expansion by 2, filtering by h[n], and compression by 2 reduces exactly to ordinary LTI filtering by the even polyphase component e0[n]=h[2n]; the odd branch receives only zeros. For white WSS input, Rdd[m]=σw²Σk h[2k]h[2(k+m)]. [PS6 solution p. 7]
Coprime expansion and compression factors commute. PS6 uses this plus a noble identity to collapse filtering expressed in z^6 onto the lowest-rate side. [PS6 solution pp. 5–6]

If a signal is exactly the impulse response of a second-order all-pole system, its p=2 Yule–Walker fit recovers the pole coefficients, and every coefficient added at p>2 is zero. [PS6 solution pp. 8–9]

Exact recurrence and global least-squares all-pole modeling are different: a sum of exponentials can obey a second-order recurrence after startup yet fail to be the impulse response of a pure all-pole system; then raising model order changes earlier optimum coefficients. [PS7 solution pp. 1–2]

Zero-padding a length-N sequence to 2N samples gives twice as dense samples of the same DTFT. Expanding in time by 2 instead produces a 2N-point DFT consisting of two repeats of the original N DFT samples. [PS7 solution pp. 6–7]

For a real sequence, X[k]=X*[N−k]; the DFT real part is circular-even and imaginary part circular-odd. This symmetry lets two real N-point DFTs be recovered from one complex N-point DFT. [PS8 solution pp. 3–5]

The Goertzel recursion yk[n]=x[n]+W_N^k yk[n−1] accumulates a selected bin; at n=N it yields X[N−k] under the problem’s convention. A second-order real resonator form follows by pairing conjugate factors. [PS8 solution pp. 1–2]
With length-128 blocks and a length-64 FIR, linear convolution has length 191; radix-2 FFT block filtering therefore pads both inputs to 256 points. [PS8 solution p. 6]

A stable rational system decomposes uniquely up to scale into a stable minimum-phase magnitude factor and stable all-pass factors by reflecting every outside-unit-circle zero to its conjugate reciprocal and using all-pass sections to restore the original phase/zeros. [Midterm solution pp. 2–3]

In the midterm’s C/D → expand-by-2 → H → compress-by-2 → D/C chain, the digital middle reduces to h[2n] with response (1/2)[H(e^jω/2)+H(e^j(ω/2−π))]. The overall CT system is LTI whenever sampling aliases are absent or rejected by that equivalent filter. [Midterm solution pp. 4–5]

Replacing z by z² in an FIR lattice inserts a zero-reflection stage before every original stage: expansion of h[n] by 2 maps original reflection coefficients to the even-numbered coefficients and sets odd-numbered ones to zero. [Midterm solution pp. 6–7]

An even FIR supported on −L≤n≤L is a degree-L polynomial in cosω and has at most L+1 extrema on [0,π]. Six visible extrema therefore imply L≥5 without assuming how the filter was designed. [Midterm solution pp. 8–9]

Compressing a 1024-point DFT by 2 aliases time: the 512-point IDFT is r[n]=x[n]+x[n+512]. Re-expanding those frequency samples by 2 repeats r[n] twice in time with factor 1/2. [Midterm solution pp. 10–11]
For v[n]=x[n]w[n], windowing gives V(e^jω)=(1/2π)∫X(e^jθ)W(e^j(ω−θ))dθ: multiplication by a finite window becomes periodic convolution and smooths peaks and discontinuities. [Lecture 17 p. 1]

After sampling with period T and taking an N-point DFT, bin k corresponds to continuous-time angular frequency Ω_k=2πk/(NT), provided the anti-aliasing and CT/DT mapping assumptions hold. [Lecture 17 p. 1]

A window’s main-lobe width controls spectral smearing/resolution while sidelobe height controls leakage. Raising Kaiser β widens the main lobe and lowers sidelobes; at fixed β, increasing length narrows the main lobe and lowers sidelobes at the cost of a longer DFT. [Lecture 17 p. 2]

Zero padding a fixed record samples the same DTFT more densely and can reveal picket-fence behavior, but it does not improve the ability to resolve nearby components; resolution changes only when the record/window itself changes. [Lecture 17 pp. 2–3]
For a length-L rectangularly windowed record v[n], the periodogram is I(ω)=(1/L)|V(e^jω)|², equivalently the DTFT of the finite-record autocorrelation scaled by 1/L. [Lecture 18 pp. 2–3]

The periodogram mean is the true PSD convolved with the spectral window: E{I(ω)}=(1/L)P_xx(ω)*|W(e^jω)|². It is biased for finite L but asymptotically unbiased as the normalized spectral window approaches an impulse. [Lecture 18 pp. 3–4]

Increasing periodogram record length does not force its variance to zero: var{I(ω)}≈P_xx²(ω), so the raw periodogram is not a consistent PSD estimator even though its bias vanishes asymptotically. [Lecture 18 p. 4]

Averaging K approximately independent periodograms preserves the individual estimate’s mean while reducing variance by 1/K. For a fixed total record Q=KL, more segments produce a smoother but lower-resolution estimate because each window is shorter. [Lecture 18 pp. 4–5]

Half-window overlap can nearly halve the variance relative to nonoverlapping sections for the example discussed, while a tapered window changes the associated bias/leakage behavior. [Lecture 18 pp. 6–7]

Direct computation of an N-point complex DFT requires on the order of N² complex multiplications and additions; factorizing N=p1p2…pv yields FFT work proportional to N(p1+…+pv), and radix-2 reduces this to order N log2N. [Lecture 19 pp. 1–2]

In radix-2 DIF, even frequency samples are the N/2-point DFT of x[n]+x[n+N/2], while odd samples are the N/2-point DFT of (x[n]−x[n+N/2])W_N^n. Full recursion uses (N/2)log2N complex multiplications and Nlog2N complex additions. [Lecture 19 pp. 2–3]

In radix-2 DIT, X[k]=G[k]+W_N^kH[k], where G and H are N/2-point DFTs of the even- and odd-indexed input samples. The standard flow graph has bit-reversed input and normal output; node rearrangement can exchange normal and bit-reversed ordering. [Lecture 19 pp. 3–4]

A DIF flow graph can be obtained by transposing a corresponding DIT flow graph—swap input/output and reverse every edge—linking algorithm variants through the general transposition principle. [Lecture 19 p. 4]

To compute just one coefficient X[k] of an 8-point DFT, the canonical sum needs eight complex products and can be cheaper than running a full radix-2 FFT that produces all eight coefficients. [Lecture 20 p. 1]

The Goertzel derivation uses h[n]=W_N^(−kn)u[n): filtering x[n] and reading y_k[N] gives X[k]. Factoring the pole pair gives denominator 1−2cos(2πk/N)z^−1+z^−2 and a final complex numerator operation. [Lecture 20 pp. 1–3]

For one frequency, Goertzel requires N real multiplications plus one complex multiplication in the handout’s accounting, and the same recurrence can evaluate X(e^jω) at non-bin frequencies. [Lecture 20 p. 3]

The chirp transform rewrites uniformly spaced samples X(e^j(ω0+kΔω)) as pre-modulation by one chirp, convolution with a fixed conjugate chirp, and post-modulation. Finite support makes the otherwise noncausal/unstable-looking convolution implementable by bookkeeping. [Lecture 20 pp. 3–4]
The STFT/TDFT convention in the notes is X[n,λ)=Σ_m x[n+m]w[m]e^(−jλm); time advances by sliding x past a fixed window. A magnitude plot over n and λ is a spectrogram. [Lecture 21 pp. 1–2]

For fixed n, the STFT is the frequency-domain convolution of the shifted signal spectrum with W: X[n,λ)=(1/2π)∫e^(jθn)X(e^jθ)W(e^j(λ−θ))dθ, so the usual leakage–resolution window tradeoff remains local in time. [Lecture 21 p. 2]

Sampling the STFT at N frequencies produces the N-point DFT of the windowed block. For a length-L window and time hop R, the notes give exact-reconstruction feasibility when R≤L≤N; longer windows favor frequency resolution and shorter windows favor time resolution. [Lecture 21 p. 3]

A bank of modulated prototype filters h_k[n]=e^(jω_kn)h_0[n], with w[m]=h_0[−m], produces sampled STFT channels y_k[n]=X[n,λ)|_(λ=ω_k); downsampling each channel by R removes time redundancy. [Lecture 21 pp. 3–4]

Polyphase decomposition lets all N modulated filter branches share the R input polyphase components. Relative to direct LN complex multiplies per input sample, the polyphase form requires LN/R. [Lecture 22 pp. 1–4]

At critical sampling R=N, the modulated polyphase combination is an N-point DFT across the filtered polyphase signals and can be implemented by an FFT. The stated total cost is L/N+log2N multiplications per input sample. [Lecture 22 pp. 4–5]
When L=N=R, each prototype polyphase component is one tap; when L=2N=2R, each has two taps and the notes explicitly identify time aliasing in the N-point FFT representation. [Lecture 22 pp. 5–6]

With 8-kHz sampling, requesting CT frequency samples no farther than 5 Hz apart requires N≥1600; a 1000-sample record must therefore be zero-padded, though this improves grid spacing rather than window-limited resolution. [PS9 solution, Problem 9.1, p. 1]

Multiplying selected DFT bins by an ideal-looking binary mask does not implement ideal DTFT low-pass filtering between those bins. Subsequent decimation can alias the unconstrained inter-bin spectrum even when the retained DFT samples look correct. [PS9 solution, Problem 9.3, pp. 2–5]

For a windowed complex sinusoid, the largest-bin estimate has worst-case angular-frequency error π/(NT). Generalized-linear-phase information can refine it via ω0=ω_hat+2∠X_w[k_hat]/(M−1), under the main-lobe/sign conditions developed in the solution. [PS9 solution, Problem 9.4, pp. 6–7]

The IDFT of N evenly spaced periodogram samples is a periodically aliased version of the aperiodic record autocorrelation. For a length-L segment, N≥2L−1 prevents overlap and makes the sampled-spectrum and continuous-periodogram autocorrelation expectations agree over the supported lags. [PS9 solution, Problem 9.6, pp. 10–12]

In the PS9 estimator-identification exercise, main-lobe width reveals actual segment length, sample density reveals zero padding, variance reveals averaging, and the number of extrema distinguishes low- versus higher-order all-pole models. [PS9 solution, Problem 9.7, p. 12]
A modulated filter bank and a DFT of x[n]w[n] agree at time zero when the analysis window is the time reversal of the prototype: w[n]=h_0[−n]. [PS10 solution, Problem 10.1, p. 1]

Samples of a 256-point windowed z-transform on radius 0.9 can be produced by a causal modulated filter bank using h_0[n]=0.9^(n−256) for 1≤n≤256, modulation ω_k=−2πk/256, and output sample N_k=256. [PS10 solution, Problem 10.2, p. 2]

For the analyzed modulated filter bank, perfect reconstruction requires the desired (l=0) channel sum to equal R and every l=1,…,R−1 alias-component channel sum to vanish for all ω. [PS10 solution, Problem 10.4(d), pp. 4–5]

The discrete-time Hilbert transformer has response −j on 0<ω<π and +j on −π<ω<0; it maps cos(ω0n) to sin(ω0n), sin(ω0n) to −cos(ω0n), and an ideal lowpass sinc to (1−cos(ω_cn))/(πn). [PS11 solution, Problem 11.3, pp. 2–3]

Two all-pass branches whose phases differ by ±π/2 form a 90-degree splitter: w[n]=y1[n]+jy2[n] has zero negative-frequency spectrum and magnitude 2|X(e^jω)| over positive frequencies. [PS11 solution, Problem 11.4, pp. 3–4]
For an echo h[n]=δ[n]+αδ[n−n0], |α|<1, the complex cepstrum is an impulse train h_hat[n]=Σ_(k≥1)(−1)^(k+1)α^kδ[n−kn0]/k. [PS11 solution, Problem 11.5, pp. 4–5]

For a minimum-phase sequence, both x[n] and its complex cepstrum are causal. The cepstrum starts with x_hat[0]=log x[0] and the supplied convolution identity yields a causal recursion in which x_hat[n] depends only on x[0…n] and earlier cepstral samples. [PS11 solution, Problem 11.6, pp. 5–6]

For a real sequence, log-magnitude is even and unwrapped phase is odd, so the complex log spectrum is conjugate symmetric and the complex cepstrum is real; time reversal of x reverses its complex cepstrum. [PS11 solution, Problem 11.7, pp. 6–7]

The project warns that severe IIR specifications can place many poles near z=1, making direct-form coefficient quantization unstable even in floating point; pairing poles and zeros into stable second-order sections and cascading them is the prescribed workaround. [Projects handout p. 5]

Project II fixes the input rate at 44.1 kHz, appends decimation by four to 11.025 kHz, and limits the design to 17 multiplications per input sample; polyphase cost must be compared with high-rate direct cost for six IIR/FIR families. [Projects handout pp. 5–7]

The final’s DFT/correlation problem reinforces that IDFT{|X_N[k]|²} is a circularly aliased autocorrelation: the full autocorrelation of a 1024-sample record needs N≥2047, while lags |m|≤10 can be recovered already at the allowed minimum N=1024 by taking the corresponding head/tail circular indices. [Final exam Problem 7 pp. 20–21; solution scan pp. 22–23]

A first-order recursion y[n]=x[n]+ay[n−1] can evaluate one DTFT frequency: choosing a=e^(j2π/60) and sampling at any multiple of 60 greater than 89—e.g. M=120—makes y[M]=X(e^jω)|_(ω=2π/60) for a 90-sample input. [Final exam Problem 9 p. 24; solution scan p. 26]
pedagogy: MIT 6.341 is a compact, proof-conscious graduate course whose terse lecture handouts are inseparable from demanding problem sets, worked solutions, exams, and empirical projects. It assumes fluent signals-and-systems foundations—DTFT, z-transform, LTI systems, sampling, random processes, complex variables, and linear algebra—and uses the opening weeks as both review and diagnostic. New material is typically introduced through a provocative question, a counterintuitive spectrum, an operation-count comparison, or a system that appears equivalent until rate, phase, causality, or finite precision is examined. Derivations move deliberately among time, frequency, z-plane, signal-flow, matrix, and implementation views; textbook figures are often referenced rather than re-explained. The problem sets do most of the pedagogical heavy lifting: students prove identities, build counterexamples, sketch spectra, track poles and zeros, count operations, reverse-engineer estimators, and justify exact reconstruction or system equivalence. Solutions are unusually explicit about tempting wrong arguments, nonuniqueness, indexing, and edge cases. A recurring course habit is to make the student name the relevant notion of efficiency and distinguish ideal infinite-precision algebra from realizability, numerical robustness, aliasing, leakage, quantization, and finite-word-length noise. The later lectures are organized around spectral-analysis misconceptions and algorithm choice, culminating in a unified view of the STFT as sliding-window DFT, modulated filter bank, polyphase network, and FFT. Projects extend the mathematics into listening and design: students test phase audibility, compare six denoising-filter families, confront software conventions and second-order-section stability, and satisfy a hard multiplier budget using multirate structure. Closed-book, calculator-free exams reward concise demonstrated reasoning under the E/G/R/M/U understanding scale rather than answer-only work.

gems: Lecture 2, pp. 2–3: the notes distinguish positive magnitude plus discontinuous phase from signed amplitude plus a straight phase line; the same FIR response becomes far easier to interpret by moving π flips into the amplitude.
Lecture 2, p. 3: MATLAB's wrapped plot of the perfectly linear phase -2ω is a compact debugging trap—nothing nonlinear happened to the system, only to the display convention.
Lecture 2, pp. 5–6: a symmetry center α may fall halfway between samples; the impulse response is still exactly symmetric even though no sample lies at its center.
Lecture 3, p. 6: 'minimum phase' earns its name twice: it has both minimum pointwise group delay and the fastest cumulative energy arrival among equal-magnitude causal responses.

Lecture 4, p. 3: a fractional sample delay cannot be interpreted as x[n-Δ]; it becomes an infinite shifted-sinc convolution, a clean example of a simple frequency response hiding a nonlocal time-domain operator.

Lecture 5, pp. 1–3: decimation is not merely throwing samples away—the frequency-domain formula shows M shifted, compressed copies being averaged, which makes aliasing inevitable unless the band is first narrowed.
Lecture 6, p. 4: doubling the oversampling factor buys exactly one-half bit in the simple white-noise model, a memorable engineering exchange rate.

Lecture 6, pp. 4–5: the first-order shaper feeds back the previous quantization error; slowly varying error nearly cancels, while rapid error is deliberately amplified where the later lowpass can discard it.

Lecture 7, pp. 6–20: an eighth-order direct-form bandpass becomes unstable at 12- or 10-bit coefficient precision as poles cross the unit circle, while alternative realizations of the same ideal transfer function remain usable.

Lecture 8, p. 2: the IIR/FIR comparison refuses a simplistic 'lower order means cheaper' rule—operation count must be measured per input, output, or unit time, and a polyphase FIR can beat a nominally lower-order IIR.
Lecture 8, pp. 4–5: every Butterworth zero sits at z=-1, so the numerator (1+z^{-1})^N can be built as repeated delay-and-add stages with no coefficient multipliers.
Lecture 8, pp. 7–8: elliptic approximation spends ripple in both bands to obtain the lowest rational order; it is the sharpest explicit demonstration of trading smoothness for implementation cost.
PS1 solution, Problem 1.10, pp. 8–9: three narrowband packets act as probes—one vanishes, while the other two independently reveal ≈1.8/40-sample and ≈1.7/80-sample gain-delay behavior.
PS2 solution, Problem 2.9, pp. 11–13: testing consistent resampling with a single shifted impulse collapses a complicated continuous reconstruction/resampling chain to h_1(nT-n_0T_1)=δ[n-n_0].
PS2 solution, Problem 2.7, p. 10: changing speech from 5 kHz to 3 kHz becomes the concrete rational factor 3/5—expand by 3, lowpass to π/5 with gain 3, then decimate by 5.
PS3 solution, Problem 3.1, p. 1: positive group delay everywhere still does not imply causality; the half-sample delay e^{-jω/2} is the one-line counterexample.

PS3 solution, Problem 3.5, pp. 3–5: moving from first- to second-order shaping changes retained low-frequency noise from a quadratic to quartic zero and yields the striking M^{-5} in-band variance law.

PS4 solution, Problem 4.4, pp. 4–6: using one physical multiplier to set both an all-pass pole and its reciprocal zero makes an invariant structural rather than numerical—the relation survives any coefficient rounding.
PS4 solution, Problem 4.7, pp. 9–10: the lattice recursion exposes instability immediately: reflection coefficients -12/5 and -2 exceed unity, no root-solving required.
Background Exam, Problem 12 (exam p. 7; solution p. 4): a sinusoid's output phase is set by ∠H at its carrier, not by group delay; the multiple-choice distractors make the common confusion explicit.

Background Exam, Problem 7 (exam p. 4; solution p. 2): two CT tones through the same sampled differentiator produce outputs tied to aliased discrete frequency—6π and 14π rad/s do not behave as naive CT differentiation would predict.

Problem Set 1, p. 1: students report which review problems they solved unaided, self-grade a prior exam, and predict their upcoming score; the course turns prerequisite uncertainty into measured metacognition rather than hidden attrition.

A design can be mathematically optimal and still be poor: rectangular truncation minimizes integrated squared error, yet its fixed-height ripple motivates a different minimax objective. [Lecture 9 pp. 1–3]

The notes turn window lore into two physical knobs: main-lobe width sets transition width; sidelobe mass sets ripple. A smoother endpoint buys smaller ripple by spending transition sharpness. [Lecture 9 p. 2]

‘What do we mean by efficient?’ is the multirate lecture’s comeback: a manipulation can reduce multiplications while increasing expander blocks, so the cost model must be named before optimization. [Lecture 11 p. 2]
An N-tap decimator goes from N to N/M multiplies per second simply by refusing to compute samples that the compressor will throw away. [Lecture 10 pp. 1, 4–5]

The sinusoid sampling riddle answers 0 Hz: a single sinusoid below 5 kHz has only amplitude, phase, and frequency as unknowns, so three nonuniform samples can identify it and no continuing sample stream is needed. It is deliberately surprising and opens parametric modeling. [Lecture 12 p. 1]

All-pole modeling replaces a nonlinear output mismatch with a convenient inverse-filter error; the freedom to choose the error criterion is what makes the normal equations appear. [Lecture 12 pp. 1–3]
Levinson–Durbin is presented as algebra with a structural payoff: intermediate recursion coefficients are not bookkeeping waste but the actual lattice reflection coefficients. [Lecture 13 pp. 1, 5–6]

The five opening DFT warnings are memorable: the DTFT cannot be computed, the DFT can, the DFT is not the DTFT, the FFT is not the DFT, and the FFT is not always the best way to compute its result. [Lecture 15 p. 1]

Putting a finite sequence around a cylinder makes periodic extension, circular shift, and circular convolution literal rotations and wraparound rather than abstract modulo arithmetic. [Lecture 15 p. 5; Lecture 16 pp. 3–4]
A same-looking signal assigned length 5 versus length 10 has different DFT values because the DFT samples a different grid and implies a different periodic extension. [Lecture 15 p. 5]

Overlap-save’s ‘corrupted but useful’ insight: circular convolution need not be globally alias-free; discard the first P−1 wrapped samples and keep the remaining L−P+1 exact samples. [Lecture 16 pp. 3–5]

The Euler mapping comparison gives a clean stability lesson: backward Euler preserves analog stability automatically, while forward Euler may not, even though both improve as T shrinks. [PS5 solution pp. 2–3]

A multistage-decimator design turns a 5069-tap-style burden into 284 multiplies per output by widening the early transition band, exploiting symmetry, and computing before samples are discarded only when necessary. [PS5 solution pp. 8–10]

A ‘near miss’ filter that is almost a function of z^6 becomes efficient by splitting off one awkward term in parallel; systematic polyphase decomposition reveals that several branches are exactly zero. [PS6 solution pp. 5–6]
Expansion-filter-compression can erase half a filter: after ↑2 and ↓2, the odd polyphase branch receives zero forever and the whole system is just h[2n]. [PS6 solution p. 7]

Two sums of exponentials expose a subtle modeling distinction: one is a pure two-pole impulse response and keeps its fitted coefficients at higher orders; the other has a numerator transient, so global least-squares coefficients keep changing even though its tail obeys the same recurrence. [PS6 solution pp. 8–9; PS7 solution pp. 1–2]

A 256-bin brick-wall mask inside overlap-save is not an ideal frequency-selective filter: its IDFT is finite, while a truly ideal frequency cutoff requires an infinite impulse response. [PS7 pp. 1–2; solution pp. 9–10]

The DFT transformation-matching exercise separates two operations often conflated: zero padding doubles frequency-grid density, while time expansion repeats the original frequency samples twice. [PS7 solution pp. 5–7]

Two real DFTs can hitchhike in one complex DFT by packing one sequence into the real part and the other into the imaginary part, then teasing them apart with circular even/odd symmetry. [PS8 solution pp. 3–4]

The exam’s ‘treasure chest’ filter asks for an order bound from a plotted response alone: count six extrema, invoke the polynomial-in-cosω limit, and conclude L≥5 without assuming Parks–McClellan. [Midterm pp. 10–11; solution pp. 8–9]

The midterm explicitly tells students that later parts may be solvable independently and grades understanding on an E/G/R/M/U scale, making reasoning more valuable than a lucky final value. [Midterm p. 1]

The lattice-expansion exam problem is a trap for brute force: replace z by z² and insert zero-reflection stages, so original coefficients simply occupy even lattice indices. [Midterm pp. 8–9; solution pp. 6–7]

Frequency-domain decimation of a 1024-point DFT folds the two 512-sample time halves together; frequency-domain expansion then creates two half-amplitude copies. This makes Fourier duality operational and testable. [Midterm pp. 12–13; solution pp. 10–11]

The shard opens spectral analysis with a trap: a 64-bin DFT can show two perfectly clean lines while the finite record’s DTFT has energy almost everywhere and happens to be zero at every sampled in-between bin. [Lecture 17 pp. 2–3]

‘Three illusions’ compress the unit into a durable diagnostic: invisible between bins does not mean absent; denser zero padding does not mean better resolution; and more random-process data does not make one raw periodogram converge. [Lecture 18 p. 1]
White-noise periodograms from L=16 through L=1024 keep fluctuating around the flat truth, making inconsistency visible rather than merely algebraic. [Lecture 18 p. 4]

The fixed-data-record example makes estimator design a resource allocation problem: spend samples on longer windows for sharper peaks or on more segments for lower variance—you cannot maximize both. [Lecture 18 pp. 5–7]

For N=1024, the notes contrast roughly 10^6 direct DFT operations with roughly 10^4 radix-2 FFT operations, turning the asymptotic gain into an immediately memorable two-order-of-magnitude example. [Lecture 19 p. 2]
Lecture 20 begins with an algorithm-selection ambush: asking only for X[5] of an 8-point DFT makes the celebrated FFT a needlessly expensive choice. [Lecture 20 p. 1]

The chirp transform is presented not as a historical curiosity but as a hardware-friendly way to move an analysis arc around the unit circle while reusing one fixed convolution block. [Lecture 20 p. 4]
A speech fragment—‘should we chase …’—motivates why one global spectrum is the wrong object for speech; spectral locality changes with sound class over time. [Lecture 21 p. 1]

The final two posted lectures make three representations click into one object: sliding-window DFT samples, outputs of a modulated filter bank, and an FFT across filtered polyphase components. [Lectures 21–22]

PS9 makes students identify estimators from their visual fingerprints rather than from formulas: zero padding changes dot density, averaging changes roughness, segment length changes peak width, and model order changes the count of extrema. [PS9 Problem 9.7; solution p. 12]

A plausible ‘ideal lowpass’ made by zeroing DFT bins is dismantled carefully: it constrains only the samples and can leave enough stopband energy between them to alias after downsampling. [PS9 solution Problem 9.3, pp. 2–5]

Problem Set 11 is officially ‘Due: Never’ but the handout immediately says the final assumes it has been done—a compact bit of course culture attached to serious Hilbert/cepstrum material. [PS11 p. 1]
The echo model h[n]=δ[n]+αδ[n−n0] becomes an infinite, regularly spaced cepstral impulse train, a clean demonstration of why echoes are conspicuous in quefrency. [PS11 solution Problem 11.5, pp. 4–5]

Project I directly tests the folk theorem that the ear is insensitive to phase by comparing N=1 and N=50 all-pass speech filters and asking students to describe what they actually hear. [Projects handout pp. 2–3]

The denoising project compares Butterworth, both Chebyshev types, elliptic, Parks–McClellan, and Kaiser designs under identical audible-speech goals, forcing theoretical response differences into pole-zero, impulse, group-delay, cost, and listening evidence. [Projects handout pp. 4–5]
The hardware story gives the computational constraint personality: only 17 multipliers are available because the 18th is already committed to digital volume control. [Projects handout p. 6]

Project II’s 52 individualized noisy utterances turn a common filter-design assignment into a small blind listening investigation: each student must denoise their own file and discover what it says. [Projects handout p. 7; project2.zip]
The course refuses code-dump grading: project reports summarize method and plots, explicitly exclude MATLAB code, and use the EGRMU scale to judge understanding and effort. [Projects handout pp. 1–2]

The final casts Parks–McClellan uniqueness as a treasure-chest dispute: two entrants use different declared N values yet produce the same response, and students must reconcile that with the alternation theorem. [Final Problem 4 pp. 12–15; solution scan pp. 14–16]

The scanned final solution is itself evidence of the assessment philosophy: it contains a fully worked 100-point exam graded 98 under EGRMU-style marks, with reasoning written directly into the booklet rather than an answer key alone. [Final solution scan pp. 3–26]
